title: Why Starbucks AI Tools Could Threaten Microsoft (MSFT) Stock - MarketWise
content: Listen to the audio version of this article (generated by AI). For investors, the potential $725 billion in artificial intelligence (“AI”) spending for this year no longer looks preposterous. Add that figure to the tab of what the biggest hyperscalers have already spent, and we’re talking about trillions of dollars in future spending. This has become a “must-have” strategy to benefit from the massive AI boom. If giants like Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOGL) are right, we’ll look back at all the money spent and see how it was obviously the smart bet. This has investors zeroed in on the big AI investments… The thought is that any signs of a pullback in hyperscaler spending could be disastrous for the AI story. But that’s not the main thing investors need to pay attention to right now. At least, that’s not where the signal is for whether the AI trade is working (or not)… Instead, a tech transformation at America’s largest coffee chain could spark a major shift in the AI story – and it may mean serious trouble for some of the biggest players in enterprise-technology products and services. Starbucks (SBUX) is in the midst of a turnaround. CEO Brian Niccol took over in 2024 and immediately faced several headwinds. Earnings were falling, certain stores were underperforming, and costs were rising. That’s why he made a plan to cut $2 billion in annual spending by the end of 2028. A good portion of that cost-cutting will come from lowering headcount, reducing available menu items by 30%, and changing future store models to a smaller footprint. All of this can help Starbucks return to growth. But a small portion of that $2 billion could do more than just help the coffee maker thrive in the future. Around $400 million will go toward reducing the company’s reliance on Big Tech. Right now, Starbucks relies on software from Microsoft and IBM (IBM) for inventory management and maintenance. Microsoft provides the inventory-management software, and IBM handles maintenance. It’s easy money for those companies to collect. And before AI models started popping up, Starbucks likely wouldn’t even consider getting rid of these legacy partnerships. The cost would be too great to replicate in-house. That was the backbone of the software companies’ value proposition for years: It’s easier and cheaper for you to let someone else do it. Starbucks wants to use AI to develop its own inventory-tracking and maintenance system. The company believes its engineers can do it and has set a target date for the end of next year to complete the initial rollout. If successful, Starbucks would save up to $400 million. More importantly, though, any large retailer can try to copy its new model. It would be proof that AI can scale across global businesses to reduce costs, and it could pose a major problem for software giants like Microsoft. Now, before you go dumping your shares of the AI giants, this won’t be a “wave the wand for success” type of change. This isn’t the first time Starbucks has tried to use AI to improve its inventory situation. In September 2025, it implemented an AI program across its North American stores. The company was using an AI system from NomadGo. It involved lidar sensors, cameras, and augmented reality to count inventory. Starbucks has been dealing with shortages for years. And the CEO was hoping AI would help solve that issue. NomadGo claimed 99% accuracy and 8 times the speed of standard inventory counting. But that didn’t work out when put to the test. According to Reuters, Starbucks canceled the program at more than 11,000 locations in May after the app kept miscounting inventory or mislabeling certain products. It couldn’t tell the difference between oat milk and regular milk. Employees had to go behind the system and recount inventory. And it would miss some products on the shelf altogether. NomadGo’s AI program turned out to be a failure for Starbucks. It’s also unclear if its in-house AI system will be able to replace Microsoft and IBM. What we do know is that Starbucks, like every other major company right now, is focusing on how to best use AI to reduce costs and become more efficient. It’s also worth wondering whether investing in AI will be worth it. Consulting firm McKinsey hit a nerve with this megatrend. It released a report in November 2025 stating that roughly 9 out of 10 businesses were using AI in at least one business segment. Yet, 94% of those companies reported no material benefit from AI spending. Now, the end of 2025 is essentially a millennium ago in the AI story. Since then, we’ve seen models like Anthropic’s Claude include memory functions. And large language models keep improving. Nonetheless, if the hyperscalers are going to win, they must solve the puzzle of how to make money for clients. They know it and are doing everything they can to make their and their clients’ investments worthwhile. That’s why we’re seeing OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon (AMZN), and now Microsoft enlist tech armies to solve this problem. Each company is sending teams of engineers to help clients integrate AI faster and more efficiently to improve their businesses. In June, Amazon announced that it’s spending $1 billion to build a team of thousands of Amazon Web Services (“AWS”) engineers to help its customers deploy agentic-AI solutions. The team operates under the name Forward Deployed Engineering. Microsoft is also spending $2.5 billion on a 6,000-member army under the Microsoft Frontier Company name. The goal is clear (and obvious)… to demonstrate the value of Microsoft’s services and make money for its clients. This all leaves us with two important things to watch for in the next 12 to 18 months… The first is Starbucks achieving complete success with its in-house AI system and eliminating Microsoft and IBM. In this case, look for AI adoption to bear fruit across the business world. Some major software players will be at risk of losing business. The second is Microsoft’s army of engineers actually managing to make clients money. The company becomes stickier as businesses recognize the value of its services. For Starbucks, the company’s turnaround plan is working. It beat earnings estimates in the latest quarter. And it’s climbing out of a period of falling earnings while also raising guidance for 2026. If it can get AI to further reduce costs, this will likely send the stock even higher. Starbucks recently broke out to its highest price in more than a year. The company also has a “B” grade from our Stansberry Score. This rates a company based on financials, capital efficiency, and valuation. Then it combines those scores to give an overall grade. Starbucks has an “A” in financials, an “A” in capital efficiency, and a “C” in valuation… This puts Starbucks in the top 20% of stocks in the Stansberry Score universe. As for Microsoft, the company is fighting to prove that it can remain dominant even as AI threatens to replace certain software packages. So far, the future threats remain just that – threats. Microsoft’s business is still strong. The company brought in $73 billion in free cash flow (“FCF”) over the 12 months ending in March. It also grew revenue 17.9% over that period. And earnings per share climbed 22%. That’s why it’s no surprise that Microsoft has a similar rating to Starbucks, according to our Stansberry Score. Microsoft has an “A” for financials, an “A” for capital efficiency, and a “C” for valuation. Its overall grade is a “B.” Put simply, the death of Microsoft is far from written in stone. In fact, it has the money and the elite team to tackle the problems it faces today. The AI story is constantly changing. The big winners will be the ones who can adapt to these changes quickly. Starbucks is adapting by using AI to improve its systems at a lower cost. And Microsoft is evolving in order to remain a tech giant for decades to come. Microsoft even has its own AI services, such as Copilot, Azure AI – a platform for building and managing AI applications – and data centers. Savvy investors will pay attention to the coming months and years, as they’ll play a pivotal role in deciding where both companies are positioned for the future. title: Microsoft Stock Rises 2.9% as AI Sales Push Targets OpenAI and Anthropic - TradingView
content: Microsoft MSFT, the world's largest software company, is preparing its sales team to compete more aggressively with Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind Claude, and OpenAI, another major AI developer. During internal meetings held Tuesday and Wednesday, Microsoft executives said the company should emphasize its lower costs, stronger security controls, and broader product offering. Executive Vice President Jay Parikh said Microsoft's fiscal 2027 sales message should focus on the company providing a complete end-to-end system while competitors offer individual parts. This strategy supports Microsoft's effort to position itself as a platform where businesses can fine-tune, deploy, and monitor artificial intelligence across their operations. The competitive push comes as Microsoft faces pressure from large AI startups and rival cloud platforms, including Alphabet GOOGL, the technology company that owns Google. Investors have raised concerns that newer AI tools could replace established software products, while Microsoft's rising data-center spending has added further pressure on sentiment. The stock has fallen 20% this year, although shares gained 2.9% to $396.08 by 1:50 p.m. in New York, representing the largest intraday increase in two weeks. Executive Vice President Jacob Andreou also compared Microsoft's Copilot assistant with Anthropic's Claude for use in Microsoft's office products, saying Claude was slower, less accurate, and lacked suitable security integrations. Anthropic declined to comment. Chief Executive Officer Satya Nadella said customers are expected to focus more heavily over the next year on monitoring AI costs and using cheaper models. Nadella pointed to Unilever, a consumer goods company, which built an automated claims-processing system on Microsoft's platform that is projected to generate about $300 million in savings. The system had previously used one of the most advanced AI models available before switching to a less expensive Microsoft model. Microsoft has also replaced advanced models from OpenAI and Anthropic with its own cheaper alternative in some products, according to Bloomberg. Investors may view the strategy as an attempt to improve AI economics while strengthening Microsoft's position against fast-growing competitors. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. title: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Stock Rallies Against Nasdaq Slide Despite AI Spending Discount - TechStock²
content: Microsoft shares climbed 1.8% in Thursday afternoon trading. The advance extended Wednesday’s 2.8% gain. Meanwhile, the Nasdaq Composite fell about 1% during a chip-led selloff. The stock has gained 4.6% since Tuesday’s close. Using Microsoft’s latest market capitalization, that move added about $132 billion. The divergence is the investor signal. Price action suggests traders are separating enterprise AI revenue from chip-cycle risk. Semiconductor shares fell sharply Thursday, despite continued spending on AI infrastructure. Three brokerages cut Microsoft targets on Wednesday. Each retained a positive rating. A fourth firm raised its objective. Citigroup NYSE:C analyst Tyler Radke lowered his target to $570 from $620. He called Microsoft “increasingly strategically positioned” as customers optimize AI-token spending. Barron’s The four targets published Wednesday ranged from $490 to $625. That implies 22% to 55% upside from Thursday’s price. Price targets are forecasts, not assured returns. Microsoft’s price-to-earnings ratio is 18.7% below the peers’ simple average. That discount makes the July 29 earnings report a capital-efficiency test. Azure revenue rose 40% in Microsoft’s fiscal third quarter. Growth was 39% at constant currency, excluding exchange-rate effects. Management guided for 39% to 40% constant-currency growth this quarter. AI demand is visible elsewhere. Microsoft’s AI revenue run rate exceeded $37 billion and grew 123%. Paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats passed 20 million. But spending remains the valuation brake. Third-quarter capital expenditure, or capex, reached $31.9 billion. That was roughly twice the quarter’s $15.8 billion of free cash flow. Management expects fourth-quarter capex above $40 billion. Its calendar-2026 plan is roughly $190 billion, including $25 billion from higher component prices. Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said Microsoft remained “confident in the return on these investments.” Microsoft Risks remain clear. Higher component costs could prolong margin pressure. Capacity shortages may delay revenue, while Copilot adoption could lose momentum. Competitive gains by Alphabet or Amazon would raise the earnings hurdle. The July 29 report therefore needs more than an Azure beat. Investors need AI revenue growth to outrun capital intensity. That is the clearest route to closing Microsoft’s valuation discount. content: Microsoft Corp.’s shares rose 1.5% on Monday, bucking the market-wide selloff linked to a fresh escalation in the U.S.-Iran conflict. After emerging as one of the weakest performers in its peer group during the first half of 2026, the stock has gained fresh momentum in July, catching the attention of retail traders. On Monday, Microsoft announced a major update to its iconic Search Box in Windows 11 that aims to make the experience better and less cluttered. The new search provides more accurate results by prioritizing on-device information and files before reaching the web, and a streamlined interface free of recommended content and ads. Currently, the search menu shows recent searches alongside several tiles in the right pane, including the image of the day, daily quizzes, trending searches, and game recommendations. The revamped search will display only recent searches. Microsoft said it is cleaning up web results as well. The search menu will surface the “most relevant answer” first, rather than showing “related products and promotions.” The experience is rolling out to Windows insiders in the Experimental Channel, Microsoft’s early-access testing channel. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for MSFT remained ‘bearish’ as of late Monday, with traders eyeing $400 as a crucial breakout level. “$MSFT I’ll go long on Microsoft when it breaks $400. Until then, bearish pattern! People don’t realize you can make money playing both puts and calls,” a trader said. Another wrote: “$MSFT dipping under $400 today has plenty of people watching the tape closer than usual. When a name this size pulls back, the question everyone starts asking is where the big money starts stepping back in. Worth tracking here.” MSFT stock gained nearly 5% in July to $390.99. Shares of Rocket Lab (RKLB) rose 1% overnight late Monday after the company completed a full-duration burn of Neutron’s second-stage engine, clearing another key milestone ahead of the rocket’s first launch. RKLB stock declined 5% on Monday, logging its sixth consecutive session in the red. Rocket Lab said its Archimedes Vacuum (AVac) engine completed a full-duration burn, calling the test “a thing of beauty” on X. The engine produces about 1.2 times the thrust of the first-stage Archimedes variant and is 2.5 meters taller because of its extended nozzle, which is designed for operation in space. Ground testing used a shorter nozzle section to avoid airflow instability at sea level and to help engineers model how the full engine will perform under vacuum conditions. Rocket Lab said that the work is “critical preparation for Neutron’s first flight.” CEO Peter Beck told Stocktwits in April that Rocket Lab was “pushing very hard” to launch Neutron by the fourth quarter of 2026. “We’re on track, but you know it is a rocket program at the end of the day,” Beck said. He said that the challenge is not only reaching orbit, but proving Neutron can return and be reused. “If we just had to go up, it’s super easy, we’d be in orbit by now,” Beck said. The engine milestone comes after Rocket Lab’s successful Victus Haze mission for the U.S. Space Force. Rocket Lab launched the mission 16 hours and 42 minutes after receiving notice, commissioned its Pioneer spacecraft within 38 hours and completed rendezvous and proximity operations in under 59 hours. The mission was notable since Rocket Lab provided the launch vehicle, spacecraft and orbital operations under a single contract. Beck said that the company had set “the new standard in responsive space.” Rocket Lab is expected to continue operating the Pioneer spacecraft for additional Space Force exercises in orbit. Earlier this month, Rocket Lab also agreed to acquire Iridium for about $8 billion, combining Rocket Lab’s launch and spacecraft manufacturing businesses with Iridium’s global communications network and more than 2.55 million subscribers. Beck called the combined company a “fully integrated self-launching space superpower.” On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for RKLB was ‘bearish’ amid a 675% surge in 24-hour message volumes. title: What Does Microsoft's Recent Insider Purchase Signal - Kavout | AI
content: A significant insider purchase at Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) has caught the market's attention, with Director John W. Stanton acquiring 5,000 shares on February 18, 2026. This substantial transaction, valued at $1.99 million at an average price of $397.35 per share, represents a 6.34% increase in Stanton's direct holdings, bringing his total to 83,905 shares. Such a move by a board member often acts as a powerful behavioral signal, suggesting that those closest to the company believe the stock is undervalued or poised for future appreciation. The timing of this purchase is particularly interesting, occurring as MSFT shares closed at $399.60 on February 18, up 0.69% for the day, but still significantly off its 52-week high of $555.45. Insider buying, especially of this magnitude, is widely interpreted as a bullish indicator because it demonstrates that executives are putting their own capital on the line, rather than just offering verbal endorsements. It implies a strong conviction in the company's near-term prospects and a belief that the current market price does not fully reflect its intrinsic value. This specific purchase stands out against a backdrop of predominantly insider selling at Microsoft over the past six months. While one director's buy might seem like a drop in the bucket for a company with a $2.97 trillion market capitalization, it's the qualitative signal that matters. When a director, who possesses intimate knowledge of the company's operations and strategic direction, makes a personal investment of this size, it can often precede positive developments or a turnaround in market sentiment. Historically, academic research suggests that insider purchases tend to be more informative than sales. While sales can be motivated by various personal financial reasons, a purchase typically stems from a belief in the company's future performance. This particular buy by John W. Stanton, a seasoned director with a substantial existing stake, could be a key piece of the puzzle for investors trying to gauge Microsoft's trajectory in the current challenging tech environment. While John W. Stanton's $1.99 million purchase is noteworthy, it's crucial to contextualize it within Microsoft's broader insider trading landscape. Over the past six months, insider activity for MSFT has shown a clear imbalance: 1 purchase versus 10 sales. This trend of net selling is further highlighted by a net insider sell-off of approximately $6.27 million over the last 90 days, with executives accounting for the entirety of these disposals. Prominent sales include CEO Satya Nadella, who offloaded 149,205 shares for an estimated $75.32 million across six transactions in September 2025. Similarly, Vice Chair and President Bradford L. Smith sold 38,500 shares for approximately $19.97 million in November 2025. Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft Commercial, also sold 12,750 shares for $6.27 million in December 2025. These significant sales by top executives suggest a different sentiment compared to Stanton's recent buy. Academic studies on insider trading often emphasize that while aggregate insider buying can be a strong predictor of future stock returns, aggregate selling is less informative due to diverse personal motivations. Josef Lakonishok and Lee Inmoo's 1998 research, for instance, found that insider purchases are generally more informative than sales. This suggests that while the volume of selling has been higher, Stanton's purchase carries a disproportionately stronger signal of conviction. Therefore, Stanton's buy appears to be a contrarian move within Microsoft's recent insider activity. It's not part of a widespread buying spree by multiple insiders, but rather a singular, substantial bet against the prevailing trend of executive divestment. This makes the signal from his purchase potentially more potent, as it indicates a strong individual conviction rather than a collective sentiment that might already be priced into the stock. Microsoft's stock performance has been a mixed bag recently, with shares trading at $399.60 as of February 18, 2026. While the stock saw a modest gain of 0.69% on the day of Stanton's purchase, its broader trajectory has been challenging. MSFT is currently down 17% year-to-date and has fallen 23% over the past six months, making it the worst performer among the "Magnificent Seven" during this period. This contrasts sharply with the S&P 500, which is up 7% over the same six months. The recent pullback follows Microsoft's Q4 CY2025 earnings report on January 28, 2026, which, despite beating revenue and EPS expectations, led to a more than 10% plunge in shares. The company reported EPS of $4.14 versus $3.86 expected and revenue of $81.27 billion, up 16.7% year-over-year. However, investor concerns centered on Azure growth easing to 38% (slightly below the 39% "bogey") and record $37.5 billion in AI capital spending, with worries that escalating costs are outpacing near-term returns. Despite these headwinds, Wall Street analysts maintain an overwhelmingly bullish stance. The consensus average price target is around $591.95 to $603, implying a potential 40-50% upside from current levels. For example, Citigroup set a target of $635.00 on January 30, while D.A. Davidson maintained a Buy rating with a $650.00 target. The overall analyst recommendation is a "Moderate Buy," with 84% of 50 brokerage firms rating it a Strong Buy and 10% a Buy. This divergence between recent stock performance and analyst optimism highlights the current investment dilemma. While the market has reacted negatively to AI spending and slightly moderated cloud growth, analysts see these as necessary investments for long-term gains. Wedbush, for instance, views 2026 as "the inflection year for AI and MSFT," suggesting that any post-earnings weakness should be seen as a buying opportunity for long-term investors. Microsoft's investment narrative is heavily anchored in its dominant position across several secular growth trends, primarily cloud computing and artificial intelligence. The company's Azure cloud platform continues to be a powerhouse, with strong commercial demand and remaining performance obligations rising to approximately $625 billion, driven by large Azure commitments. This robust backlog, even with a slight deceleration in growth, underscores the sticky nature of its enterprise solutions and the ongoing digital transformation. A major catalyst is Microsoft's strategic partnership with OpenAI, which now accounts for roughly 45% of its commercial remaining performance obligations. The recent deal to lock in a 20% share of OpenAI's revenue through 2032 provides a material, long-duration cash-flow stream, reinforcing MSFT's upside if OpenAI monetizes broadly. This deep integration positions Microsoft to capture significant value from the burgeoning AI revolution, with its Copilot and agentic platforms expected to drive adoption across enterprise and developer segments. However, significant risks temper this bullish outlook. Microsoft's aggressive AI spending, which reached a record $37.5 billion in capital expenditures, has raised investor concerns about the cost of innovation outpacing immediate returns. Some analysts and experts warn that Big Tech may be overinvesting in AI infrastructure, potentially leading to sector multiple compression. This heavy investment has also led to a trade-off, with Microsoft allocating scarce GPU capacity toward first-party products like Copilot, effectively capping Azure growth in the short term. Furthermore, Microsoft's premium valuation, with a forward P/E ratio around 30x, leaves a limited margin of safety if growth disappoints or macroeconomic conditions deteriorate. Competition from Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud remains fierce, and rapid advancements by other AI players could erode Microsoft's market position. While the company's financial strength is undeniable, investors must weigh the long-term potential of its AI flywheel against the near-term pressures of high capital expenditure and intense competition. Microsoft's current valuation and recent stock performance present a classic "buy the dip" dilemma for investors. Trading at $399.60, significantly below its 52-week high of $555.45, the stock has seen a notable pullback. This decline, coupled with the substantial insider purchase by Director John W. Stanton, could suggest an attractive entry point for long-term investors. The implicit message from Stanton's $1.99 million bet is that shares are undervalued at current levels, aligning with the sentiment of some analysts who view post-earnings weakness as a buying opportunity. The company's strong fundamentals and strategic positioning in high-growth areas like cloud and AI remain intact. Microsoft reported Q1 2026 revenues of $77.7 billion, an 18.43% increase year-over-year, demonstrating robust top-line growth. Its consistent dividend, declared at $0.91 quarterly (an annualized $3.64 with a yield of approximately 0.9%), also provides a measure of stability for income-focused investors. This combination of growth potential and shareholder returns strengthens the long-term investment case. However, the "dip" comes with caveats. The market's reaction to Microsoft's Q4 CY2025 earnings highlighted concerns over escalating AI capital expenditures and a slight moderation in Azure growth. While these are investments for future returns, they create near-term pressure on profitability and investor sentiment. The stock's premium valuation at 30x forward earnings means that any missteps in AI monetization or further deceleration in cloud growth could lead to additional volatility. For investors with a long-term horizon (3-5 years) and a tolerance for potential near-term volatility, Microsoft remains a foundational holding. Its dominant market positions, strong financials, and compelling growth prospects in AI and cloud computing create a favorable risk-reward profile. Dollar-cost averaging could be a prudent strategy to mitigate timing risk and gradually build a position, allowing investors to capitalize on any further dips while participating in the company's long-term growth trajectory. Microsoft's current standing offers a compelling narrative: a temporary market disconnect between its robust long-term potential and short-term operational challenges. Director Stanton's significant purchase underscores this conviction, suggesting that the current price may indeed be an attractive entry for patient capital. While the path forward may involve continued volatility, the underlying strength of Microsoft's business and its strategic AI investments position it for substantial future returns. title: The Company Behind Wall Street's Plumbing Is Looking To Tokenize MSFT Stock: Report - Stocktwits
content: The Depository Trust & Clearing Corp. (DTCC), the trade processor behind much of Wall Street's back-end infrastructure, reportedly plans to convert stocks such as Microsoft (MSFT) and other securities into digital tokens, marking the clearinghouse's latest step toward a fully digital Wall Street. MSFT’s price was up over 1% in the morning trade. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around MSFT remained in the ‘bearish’ zone, while chatter around it stayed at ‘normal’ levels over the past day. On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that almost 40 financial firms and tech providers, from JPMorgan Chase (JPM) and Goldman Sachs (GS) to BlackRock (BLK), Vanguard, and the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), will take part in a trial run to tokenize securities. The tokens will be stored at the clearinghouse on the blockchain and made available for trade, DTCC reportedly told the Journal. "The tokenization of assets and digital blockchain usage are a megatrend," DTCC President and CEO Frank La Salla told the Journal, adding that the company's focus is on "safety of the system, resiliency of the system, and working on ways in which we can free up trapped liquidity by using this new technology." The assets set to be tokenized also include shares of Circle Internet Group (CRCL), Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY), and iShares 0-3 Month Treasury Bond ETF (SGOV), as well as Treasuries of different tenors. CRCL’s price was up over 3% in morning trade. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around CRCL remained in the ‘bullish’ zone, while chatter stayed at ‘high’ levels over the past day. DTCC plans to formally launch its tokenization program in October, when firms that keep assets at the clearinghouse will be able to convert some of their securities into tokens, according to the report. DTCC safeguards more than $114 trillion in securities, and its subsidiaries processed securities transactions valued at $4.7 quadrillion last year, according to the report. The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) gave Depository Trust Co., a DTCC subsidiary, approval late last year to operate a tokenization service for the real-world assets it safeguards, though the scope was limited to highly liquid assets. The key for a shareholder isn’t to guess which way it will break, but to respect the magnitude of the move the market is preparing for. This isn’t just business as usual. title: Has Microsoft (MSFT) Found Its Next Growth Catalyst in AI Agents - Kavout | AI
content: Microsoft's (NASDAQ: MSFT) recent Build 2026 developer conference, held on June 2-3, 2026, in San Francisco, unveiled a comprehensive strategy to cement its leadership in the burgeoning artificial intelligence landscape. The announcements, particularly around Project Solara, the Microsoft Scout agent, and a new family of in-house MAI models, suggest a significant platform shift that could drive the company's next phase of growth. While shares closed yesterday at $416.67, down 2.66% from the prior close of $428.05, reflecting broader market jitters, these strategic AI initiatives position Microsoft to capture substantial value in the evolving enterprise and consumer AI markets, making it a compelling long-term investment. The core thesis emerging from Build 2026 is Microsoft's aggressive push from an "app-first" to an "agent-first" world. CEO Satya Nadella's vision emphasizes intelligence that users invoke rather than software they open, with AI agents working across applications, workflows, and devices. This paradigm shift, if successfully executed, could redefine how users interact with technology and how developers build solutions, potentially unlocking new revenue streams for Microsoft's Intelligent Cloud and Productivity and Business Processes segments. The company's market capitalization of $3.10 trillion underscores its existing scale, but these AI advancements indicate a proactive effort to maintain its competitive edge and expand its total addressable market. Project Solara emerged as one of the most intriguing, and perhaps most revealing, announcements from Build 2026, signaling Microsoft's intent to extend its AI platform beyond traditional PCs. Described as a "chip-to-cloud platform designed for an open, multiple agent world," Solara is an early-stage initiative focused on "agent-first devices." These are specialized hardware solutions built around AI agents rather than conventional applications, with Microsoft showcasing prototype badge and desk concept devices. The company is actively collaborating with chipmakers like Qualcomm and MediaTek on reference designs, indicating a serious commitment to this new hardware category. The significance of Project Solara lies in its potential to create entirely new form factors for computing, moving AI into the physical environments where people need it most. Imagine AI agents embedded in a badge for frontline workers in retail or healthcare, or a desk display providing ambient intelligence in an office. Microsoft's enterprise DNA is crucial here; unlike consumer AI gadgets that have struggled with clear use cases, Solara is explicitly aimed at enterprise scenarios where device management, identity, compliance, and workflow integration are paramount. This focus on business value, rather than just novelty, could accelerate adoption in industries like healthcare, retail, and finance, which Microsoft is already investigating. Steven Bathiche, CVP & Technical Fellow of Microsoft's Applied Sciences Group, emphasized that Solara aims to create more specific, contextual computers without the prohibitive cost of rebuilding the entire software stack for each new device. The platform's "just-in-time UI" capability allows agents to adapt their presentation across diverse devices and modalities, reducing developer effort. This flexibility is critical for fostering a diverse ecosystem of agent-first devices, from small, hypermobile wearables to fixed, specialized appliances. While still in its early stages, Project Solara represents a bold, long-term vision that could open up entirely new hardware and software markets for Microsoft, diversifying its revenue streams beyond the traditional Windows and Azure ecosystems. Microsoft Scout, unveiled at Build 2026, represents a significant evolution in AI assistance, moving from prompt-driven Copilot interactions to persistent, always-on background action. Positioned as Microsoft's first "Autopilot" agent for Microsoft 365, Scout is designed to work across a user's entire digital workspace – including Teams, Outlook, OneDrive, SharePoint, calendar, and local resources. Its core function is to coordinate work, prepare users for meetings, manage deliverables, and proactively identify risks, making the PC feel more attentive and intelligent. The power of Scout lies in its ability to leverage the vast "exhaust" of knowledge work already residing within Microsoft 365: messages, files, calendars, approvals, and organizational relationships. An agent with access to this rich context does not need to be "magical" to be immensely useful. For instance, Scout could surface a dormant thread that has become urgent, suggest a relevant document for work in progress, or flag a conflict before a calendar becomes impossible. This proactive, context-aware assistance aims to reduce cognitive load and enhance productivity, freeing users from mundane tasks and information retrieval. Crucially, Microsoft is emphasizing enterprise controls as central to Scout's pitch. Given its "always-on" nature and extensive access to sensitive data, trust and governance are paramount. Scout operates with enterprise-grade security, its own governed Entra identity, scoped credentials, and Microsoft Purview enforcement for sensitivity labels and data loss prevention. Access is initially limited to Microsoft's "Frontier" program, requiring specific Intune policy configuration and opt-in attestation, underscoring Microsoft's cautious, enterprise-focused rollout. This meticulous approach to security and governance is vital for gaining IT administrators' confidence, who will ultimately determine Scout's widespread adoption within organizations. Build 2026 also marked a pivotal moment for Microsoft's in-house AI capabilities, with the company announcing a family of seven new MAI (Microsoft AI) models. This expansion, following a renegotiated deal with OpenAI that loosened ties, signals Microsoft's strategic intent to own more of the AI stack and reduce its dependence on external partners. The flagship announcement was MAI-Thinking-1, described as Microsoft's first advanced reasoning model, featuring a 256k token window and designed for complex multi-step instructions and long-context reasoning. Other models include MAI-Code-1-Flash for GitHub Copilot, MAI-Image 2.5 for text-to-image and editing, MAI-Transcribe-1.5 (claimed to be five times faster than competing models), and MAI-Voice-2 with support for 15 new languages. The introduction of MAI-Thinking-1 is particularly significant because reasoning models are often seen as a proxy for a company's seriousness in the AI race. By developing its own reasoning model, Microsoft gains greater control over tuning for cost efficiency, integration into its vast product portfolio, and enterprise-specific workloads. This move allows Microsoft to offer customers flexibility through its Azure AI Foundry, while increasingly favoring its own models within Copilot and Microsoft 365 experiences. It's a strategic play to shift leverage in the AI ecosystem, making OpenAI an "optional" partner rather than an indispensable one. This internal model development is not about dethroning frontier models from OpenAI or Google DeepMind in every benchmark. Instead, it's about building a portfolio of models that can be embedded into existing Microsoft products, routed efficiently through Azure, and priced as part of a larger software relationship. For instance, MAI-Code-1-Flash is optimized for GitHub Copilot and Visual Studio Code, directly impacting developer productivity within Microsoft's ecosystem. This pragmatic approach aims to deliver useful intelligence at a sustainable cost, enhancing Microsoft's platform control and potentially improving its margins on AI-powered services. Microsoft's Build 2026 announcements collectively reinforce its formidable competitive position across cloud, AI, and software development, while also introducing new vectors for growth. The "agent-first" paradigm, spearheaded by Project Solara and Microsoft Scout, positions the company to lead the next wave of computing, moving beyond the current app-centric model. This proactive stance could create significant first-mover advantages in specialized AI devices and always-on enterprise agents, areas where rivals like Google and Amazon are also investing but perhaps without Microsoft's deep enterprise integration. The strategic development of in-house MAI models, particularly MAI-Thinking-1, strengthens Microsoft's control over its AI supply chain and reduces potential dependencies on external partners. This vertical integration allows for greater optimization of cost, performance, and security across its vast product ecosystem, from Azure to Windows and Microsoft 365. While Microsoft maintains its partnership with OpenAI, having its own robust model family provides a crucial hedge and increases its negotiating power, potentially leading to better margins and more tailored AI solutions for its enterprise customers. This diversified AI portfolio makes Microsoft a more resilient and self-sufficient player in the intensely competitive AI market. For investors, these developments underscore Microsoft's commitment to innovation and its ability to leverage its extensive ecosystem. The potential for new revenue streams from agent-first devices (Project Solara) and enhanced productivity tools (Microsoft Scout) could fuel long-term growth. Furthermore, the ability to offer a comprehensive, integrated AI stack – from chips and operating systems to cloud infrastructure and proprietary models – creates a powerful lock-in effect for enterprise customers. While the stock's current price of $416.67 is below its 52-week high of $555.45, the strategic depth of these AI initiatives suggests a strong foundation for future value creation, particularly as these agent-first platforms mature and gain wider adoption. Despite the ambitious vision, Microsoft's "agent-first" future is not without significant risks and challenges that investors should consider. The primary hurdle for Project Solara and Microsoft Scout is the critical issue of trust and governance. Giving AI agents pervasive access to enterprise data and the ability to act autonomously raises profound questions about data privacy, security, and accountability. As Dr. Ashraf Elnashar noted on LinkedIn, when agents act before being asked, the critical questions become: who authorized the action, what was its scope, and what happens when it's wrong? Microsoft's emphasis on Entra identity, Intune policy, and Purview data protections is a necessary first step, but real-world deployment will test the robustness of these controls. Another significant challenge lies in user adoption and the "social consequences" of always-on agents. While Scout promises enhanced productivity, it also risks making employees feel surveilled or overwhelmed by constant AI intervention. Microsoft has a history of sometimes overestimating user desire for AI woven into every surface. The success of Scout will depend on its ability to demonstrate clear value without feeling intrusive, requiring a delicate balance of transparency, user control, and predictable behavior. The "personality" of an agent is less important than its judgment and humility to stop when context is insufficient. Finally, the shift to agent-first devices with Project Solara faces the challenge of ecosystem development. Creating a new hardware category requires convincing developers to build for it and enterprises to invest in new infrastructure. While Microsoft's enterprise focus is a strength, the market for specialized agent devices is nascent and unproven. The company will need to demonstrate compelling return on investment for these new form factors to gain traction. These challenges highlight that while Microsoft's AI vision is bold, its execution will require careful navigation of technical, ethical, and market adoption complexities. Microsoft's Build 2026 conference laid out a compelling vision for an agent-first future, driven by Project Solara, Microsoft Scout, and a robust suite of in-house MAI models. These initiatives represent a strategic pivot to embed AI deeper into enterprise workflows and new device categories, positioning the company for long-term growth. Investors should monitor the successful implementation of governance frameworks and the pace of enterprise adoption as these ambitious AI platforms mature. Want deeper research on any stock? title: Prediction: Microsoft Stock Is Going to Soar After July 29 - The Motley Fool
content: Microsoft stock looks like a bargain heading into its upcoming quarterly earnings report. Microsoft (MSFT +1.26%) is scheduled to release its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter results (ended June 30) on July 29, and I think it could spark a recovery in the company's languishing stock, which is currently down 29% from its record high. Microsoft has been a casualty of the broader sell-off in the software sector, as investors fear that the growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) could render legacy software products obsolete. But the company is proving it can use this revolutionary technology to its advantage, not just in its software business but also in its booming cloud computing segment. Microsoft stock is heading into July 29 at a very attractive price, so here's why it could be a good long-term buy before the earnings release. Microsoft developed its own AI virtual assistant called Copilot, which it embedded in the Windows operating system, Edge internet browser, and Bing search engine for free. But it's also available as a paid add-on to the 365 productivity suite, helping users rapidly create content in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and more. Companies around the world pay for more than 400 million 365 licenses for their employees, and all of them are candidates for the Copilot add-on, so this move represents a huge financial opportunity for Microsoft. By the end of the fiscal 2026 third quarter, ended March 31, enterprises had added Copilot to 20 million licenses, up by an eye-popping 250% year over year. While pure-play AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic have to acquire customers from scratch, Microsoft can sell Copilot and other AI products into its enormous existing customer base. Therefore, while some investors believe legacy enterprise software is in trouble, Microsoft is turning its product portfolio into a huge advantage in the AI race. Copilot adoption will be closely watched by investors when the company reports its fourth-quarter results on July 29. I think further triple-digit growth could flip the opinion of some of the more bearish investors. Developing AI models from scratch requires substantial computing capacity, which is typically delivered by large data centers equipped with thousands of specialized chips. Most enterprises can't afford to build this infrastructure themselves, so they rent it from cloud computing platforms such as Microsoft Azure. Microsoft already operates data centers worldwide, but it's working to double its footprint over the next two years to meet demand for computing power from the AI industry. In fact, as of March 31, the company had a staggering $627 billion order backlog from customers who were waiting for more infrastructure to come online, and that figure doubled from the same time last year. Azure's total revenue increased by 40% year over year during the third quarter, an acceleration from the 39% growth it delivered three months earlier in the second quarter. But considering Microsoft thinks it can convert its entire $627 billion backlog into revenue over the next two and a half years, I think even faster growth could be ahead. If Microsoft shows even further growth in its order backlog on July 29, that will only increase my conviction that Azure is on track for more blockbuster quarterly revenue results. The 29% decline in Microsoft stock from its record high has pushed its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio down to just 22.9, making it substantially cheaper than the Nasdaq-100 index, which has a P/E of 34.5. In other words, Microsoft appears to be heavily undervalued compared with a basket of its big-tech peers. Its stock looks even more attractive when looking ahead. Based on Wall Street's earnings estimate for fiscal 2027 (which started on July 1), its forward P/E is 19.9. If we assume Wall Street's earnings estimate proves to be accurate, Microsoft stock would have to soar by 73% over the next 12 months just to trade in line with the 34.5 P/E ratio of the Nasdaq-100. That isn't unrealistic considering Microsoft averaged a P/E of 32.7 over the last 10 years. Simply put, investors are getting a fantastic price for Microsoft heading into its latest quarterly report on July 29. It will probably take a series of positive results over the next year or so to rebuild investors' confidence in its software business, but the rewards might be worth the wait. title: What's Behind Barclays' Continued Bullish Stance on Microsoft (MSFT) - Kavout | AI
content: Barclays has consistently maintained a "Buy" or "Overweight" rating on Microsoft, signaling a strong conviction in the tech giant's future performance. Analyst Raimo Lenschow recently reaffirmed a "Buy" rating with a $600 price target on March 10, 2026, following earlier "Overweight" ratings in December 2025 and "Buy" ratings in January and February 2026, often with a $625 price target. This sustained optimism stems from Microsoft's robust monetization strategies and its undeniable leadership in the burgeoning AI landscape. A key driver of Barclays' bullishness is Microsoft's ability to steadily monetize its product ecosystem, particularly through strategic price adjustments. The company announced upcoming price increases for its Office and Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions, effective July 1, 2026. This marks the second major price adjustment since Office 365's 2011 launch, reflecting significant expansion in product capabilities and increased value delivered to enterprise customers. Furthermore, the launch of Microsoft's $99/month E7 AI tools bundle, integrating advanced AI features like Copilot, presents a clear up-sell opportunity that Barclays views favorably. This move underscores Microsoft's strategy to leverage its AI-driven product leadership, backed by a loyal base of enterprise clients, to drive further revenue growth. The firm's confidence is rooted in Microsoft's proven track record of innovation and its capacity to translate technological advancements into tangible financial gains. Barclays’ analysis highlights Microsoft’s strong competitive position, particularly in enterprise software and cloud services, where its extensive customer base and integrated offerings create significant switching costs. This ecosystem approach, combined with strategic pricing power and continuous innovation in AI, underpins the analyst's belief that Microsoft is well-positioned for sustained growth and strong monetization potential in the coming years. Microsoft's transformation from a traditional software empire to a diversified technology platform is a testament to its strategic foresight, with its business now segmented into Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing. This diversified structure is not merely about breadth; it's a carefully orchestrated ecosystem where each segment, particularly Intelligent Cloud, plays a pivotal role in fueling the company's ambitious AI agenda. Azure, Microsoft's cloud computing arm, stands as the critical underpinning for its entire AI strategy. Azure's rapid growth is not just a standalone success story; it's the engine that powers Microsoft's generative AI capabilities, including its deep partnership with OpenAI and the widespread integration of Copilot across its product suite. Every Copilot feature in Office, every enterprise workload migrated to the cloud, and every developer tool leveraging OpenAI models, strengthens the same core infrastructure. This creates a powerful virtuous cycle: AI spending doesn't deplete the core business but rather enhances and expands it, making Azure an even more indispensable platform. The company's commitment to AI is evident in its product development. Microsoft 365, for instance, saw over 1,100 new features released in the past year across security, productivity, and Copilot functionalities. This continuous innovation increases the value proposition of its suites, justifying price increases and reinforcing customer loyalty. The strategic logic is clear: by embedding AI deeply into its existing, widely adopted products, Microsoft ensures that its AI investments yield direct benefits across its vast enterprise and consumer base. This integrated approach differentiates Microsoft from peers who might focus on more speculative, pure-play AI ventures. Microsoft's AI strategy is deeply intertwined with its established, high-margin businesses, providing a more stable and scalable path to AI monetization. The synergy between its cloud infrastructure, enterprise software, and AI services positions Microsoft as a balanced, yet potent, force in the evolving technology landscape, capable of compounding value through both growth and resilience. Microsoft's financial performance reflects a company that consistently delivers robust growth and shareholder returns, making it a cornerstone of many investment portfolios. For the trailing twelve months (TTM), Microsoft reported impressive financials: a market capitalization of $2.97 trillion, with a healthy P/E ratio of 24.92 and a P/S ratio of 9.72. These valuation metrics, while reflecting a premium for quality and growth, are supported by strong underlying profitability, with a net margin of 39.0% and an EPS of $16.05. The company's growth trajectory remains compelling. In fiscal year 2025, Microsoft achieved 14.9% revenue growth and 15.6% EPS growth year-over-year. Over a longer horizon, its 5-year cumulative growth in revenue per share stands at an astounding 101.7%, with net income per share growing by 135.4%. This consistent double-digit growth, particularly in its Intelligent Cloud segment, demonstrates Microsoft's ability to expand its market share and monetize its innovations effectively. Beyond operational growth, Microsoft is a significant player in capital returns, making it a shareholder-friendly stock. In fiscal year 2025 alone, the company distributed $24.08 billion in dividends and executed $18.42 billion in share repurchases. This makes Microsoft one of the S&P 500's largest dividend payers by total dollars, offering a quarterly dividend of $0.91 per share, translating to a 0.89% yield. Such substantial capital allocation enhances shareholder value, providing both income and a reduction in share count. Microsoft's balance sheet also remains strong, with a current ratio of 1.39 and a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.32, indicating solid liquidity and manageable leverage. The company's ability to generate significant free cash flow, despite a slight TTM decline of -3.3% in FCF growth, underpins its capacity for continued investment in R&D, strategic acquisitions, and shareholder distributions. These financial fundamentals paint a picture of a well-managed, highly profitable enterprise with a clear path for sustained value creation. Despite its formidable strengths and bullish analyst sentiment, Microsoft is not immune to significant risks and headwinds that investors must consider. The most immediate concern is its valuation. Trading at a P/E of 24.92 and a P/S of 9.72, Microsoft's stock commands a premium compared to historical standards, reflecting market expectations for continued high growth, particularly from AI. If enterprise spending were to decelerate sharply, or if the monetization of generative AI tools takes longer than anticipated, the stock could experience a significant correction. Another major challenge stems from the substantial capital expenditures required for AI data center buildouts. While these investments are crucial for future growth, they represent a significant cash burn in the near term. Public pushback over the immense electricity consumption and environmental impact of these data centers could also introduce regulatory or reputational risks. Furthermore, a reported vulnerability in Microsoft Authenticator and increased demand for downside protection in options markets reflect growing investor caution regarding security and potential market volatility. Regulatory scrutiny poses a persistent threat. Microsoft's immense size and market dominance make it a prime target for antitrust investigations in both the US and the EU. A preliminary Swiss probe into Microsoft 365 licensing, for instance, highlights the ongoing regulatory pressure the company faces. Such investigations can lead to hefty fines, restrictions on business practices, and reputational damage, potentially impacting future growth and profitability. Finally, internal factors like leadership changes can introduce uncertainty. The announced retirement of Rajesh Jha, a long-time head of experiences and devices (Office/Copilot products), creates short-term execution and transition risks. While Microsoft has a deep bench of talent, any significant leadership shift in critical divisions warrants investor attention. These combined risks, from valuation and capital intensity to regulatory oversight and internal transitions, underscore the need for a balanced perspective on MSFT's otherwise compelling investment thesis. Microsoft's position within the "Magnificent Seven" is unique; it's often seen as the most balanced bet, rather than the most speculative high-flyer. While it may not deliver the explosive, asymmetric upside of some pure-play AI or hardware companies, its diversified business model, massive scale, and consistent cash generation make it an exceptionally reliable pillar in the large-cap tech space. This balance of growth, resilience, and shareholder-friendly policies sets it apart from its peers. The company's strategic transformation has allowed it to pivot from a software empire to a comprehensive technology platform encompassing cloud computing, AI, productivity software, gaming, and professional networks. This broad exposure means Microsoft isn't reliant on the perfect execution of a single segment. If cloud growth slows, its software franchises can maintain their moats, and AI can incrementally lift productivity and pricing power across the entire portfolio. This inherent diversification provides a strong defense against market volatility and sector-specific downturns. Compared to other "Magnificent Seven" constituents, Microsoft offers a different risk-reward profile. It boasts better structural growth drivers than Apple's mature hardware ecosystem and a higher-margin, more scalable business than Amazon's retail operations. Its risk profile is also considerably less volatile than Tesla's. This makes Microsoft an ideal core holding for investors seeking steady, compounding returns rather than extreme speculative gains. Ultimately, Microsoft's strength lies in its ability to leverage its massive scale and integrated ecosystem to drive consistent, high-quality growth. It's a leveraging machine for diversified, high-margin businesses, complemented by sound capital allocation. As investors look towards 2026 and beyond, Microsoft remains one of the safest long-term plays, offering a compelling blend of innovation, financial stability, and shareholder returns that solidifies its status as a leader, albeit a more measured one, within the elite group of tech giants. Microsoft continues to be a compelling investment, balancing robust growth drivers with a strong financial foundation. While its premium valuation and ongoing capital expenditures warrant careful monitoring, the company's strategic AI integration and diversified revenue streams position it for sustained long-term success. title: Big Tech Earnings Today: MSFT, AMZN, META, GOOGL Set To Test Mag7's Incredible April Rally - Stocktwits
content: In a rare event, four of the biggest tech companies will report their quarterly results simultaneously after the market closes on Wednesday, with their financials and commentary set to shape the market and the broader AI trade. AMZN, META, MSFT and GOOGL stocks were marginally lower in early premarket on Wednesday. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘bullish’ for GOOGL, ‘bearish’ for META, and ‘neutral’ for MSFT and AMZN. The results would also test the sharp rally in the so-called Magnificent Seven stocks, which have staged a strong rebound over the past month. The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS), the fund which tracks this group, is up 15.4% and heading for its best month since its launch in December 2023. On Tuesday, over 70 Democratic lawmakers in the U.S. House called on Trump to maintain restrictions preventing Chinese automakers from entering the American market, citing national security concerns over connected-vehicle data and rising competitive pressure on the domestic auto industry, Reuters reported. The letter, led by Debbie Dingell and Ro Khanna, comes ahead of Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping next month and follows similar appeals from senators and major auto-industry groups in recent weeks. While U.S. officials said that national-security safeguards remain a priority, China’s embassy urged Washington to avoid “discriminatory” restrictions. Republican Senator Bernie Moreno separately said he plans legislation to permanently block Chinese vehicles from entering the U.S. market. At the same time, regulatory developments in China are adding another layer of uncertainty to the autonomous-driving space, which is key to Tesla’s long-term strategy. Chinese authorities recently suspended new robotaxi license approvals after 200 driverless vehicles operating under Baidu’s Apollo Go program stopped mid-traffic in Wuhan in a major traffic incident. Four central government agencies subsequently ordered a comprehensive safety self-inspection across major autonomous-driving companies following the outage. Local police said that the disruption was due to a system failure, according to a Nikkei report. The review could temporarily weigh on expectations for large-scale robotaxi deployment, even as regulators continue supporting autonomous driving over the longer term. Tesla continues to navigate regulatory and competitive pressures in China, its second-largest market and home to its largest global export hub in Shanghai. The company has been working with Baidu to improve navigation-map integration for its Full Self-Driving Version (FSD) 13 software as it adapts the system to local road conditions under strict data-localization requirements. Earlier this year, Tesla also launched a local AI training center in China to develop its assisted-driving capabilities tailored to domestic traffic environments. CEO Elon Musk recently said that the “limiting factor” for Tesla in China remains production output at its Shanghai facility ahead of broader supervised FSD approval in the country. title: MSFT Stock Drops After British Hedge Fund Slashes $8B Stake, Almost Ends Decade-Long Holding - Stocktwits
content: Microsoft (MSFT) share price eased 1% on Friday after British billionaire Christopher Hohn’s TCI Fund Management nearly liquidated most of its position in the Windows operating system developer, citing concerns that the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence could undermine the tech giant's dominance in software. TCI reduced its Microsoft holding from 10% of its portfolio at the end of 2025 to just 1% by March 2026. The move represents the offloading of an approximately $8 billion stake in the software giant, the Financial Times reported, citing a quarterly investor letter. "We reduced our investment in Microsoft because the rapid progress in AI introduces uncertainty over Microsoft’s competitive position in the future," Hohn reportedly said in the letter. "We are primarily concerned about Microsoft's Office productivity software franchise, where AI could change established workflows and lead to the emergence of new productivity platforms, but we also see some risks in Azure," he added. The decision marks a significant shift for TCI, which has been a staunch supporter of Microsoft for nearly a decade, benefiting from a roughly 400% rise in the company's share price over the past nine years. Hohn also holds stocks for an average of nine years, far longer than most other hedge fund traders typically do, in an effort to benefit from the long-term growth of high-quality stocks, FT said. TCI’s top holdings include General Motors, Visa, Moody’s, and the S&P 500. In 2026, several high-profile hedge funds have reduced their exposure to Microsoft, citing a range of reasons from valuation concerns to fears of long-term AI disruption. While Microsoft’s AI partnership with OpenAI initially fueled a massive rally, these recent exits have raised concerns around investor sentiment. Duquesne Family Office and Tiger Global are among the names that recently cut their exposure to Microsoft stock, citing AI-related disruption concerns. Microsoft enjoyed an early first-mover advantage through its partnership with OpenAI, but that move is facing a tough test as Wall Street grows impatient with the pace of AI monetization. MSFT’s amended relationship with OpenAI has also raised a few concerns. While Microsoft remains a primary partner, OpenAI is now permitted to strike cloud deals with rivals like Amazon (AWS) and Google Cloud, ending Microsoft's exclusive access to the startup's newest innovations. Microsoft is also facing intense competition in the cloud segment. While Azure grew 40% in the first quarter of 2026, it was eclipsed by Google Cloud’s 63% growth, which Google attributed to its enterprise AI solutions becoming a primary driver. Meanwhile, AWS remains the market leader with a 28% share of the worldwide cloud market. Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘bearish,’ and message volumes were ‘normal.’ One user raised concerns about the viability of investing in MSFT at the moment and highlighted the gains available in other AI-related stocks. Retail sentiment around the company on Stocktwits  remained in ‘neutral’ territory over the past day, with chatter at ‘high’ levels. The dip in Coinbase’s share price comes amid weakness in the cryptocurrency market, with Bitcoin (BTC) struggling to hold $80,000, and a slew of price target cuts from Wall Street after the company missed first quarter (Q1) earnings estimates. Meanwhile, CRCL’s stock edged 0.1% higher in morning trade, with retail sentiment trending in ‘bullish’ territory over the past day, accompanied by chatter at ‘extremely high’ levels. Retai sentiment around USDC, however, trended in ‘bearish’ territory alongside ‘normal’ levels of chatter. One of the biggest unresolved issues in negotiations remains the inclusion of ethics restrictions tied to cryptocurrency ownership and business ties among senior government officials. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said earlier this week at Consensus Miami 2026 that the legislation would not pass the Senate without those safeguards. “There will be no one voting for this bill if we don't have an ethics provision,” she stated during the event. Gillibrand warned that lawmakers, presidents, vice presidents, and senior administration officials should be prohibited from profiting from cryptocurrency businesses while in office. Bitcoin’s price was trading at around $80,300 in morning trade, down 0.1% in the last 24 hours. title: S&P 500, Dow And Nasdaq Drop As Inflation Angst Spurs Rate Hike Fears — TSLA, SBUX, POET, MSFT, NVDA In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. stock indices dropped on Friday as surging bond yields and higher-for-longer inflation metrics renewed rate hike fears amid persistently elevated oil prices. The S&P 500  fell 1.2%, the Nasdaq lost 1.5%, and the Dow Jones declined 1.1%. The Russell 2000, which tracks stocks with small market capitalizations, fell 2.4%, the index's worst day in 2026. Among ETFs tracking benchmark indexes, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) fell 1.4%, and Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) ended Friday around 2% lower, while the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) eased 1.2%. While SPY ended the week marginally higher, up 0.2%, QQQ and DIA ended the week down between 0.2% and 0.3%. Meanwhile, retail sentiment on Stocktwits for SPY, QQQ, and DIA was all in the ‘bullish’ territory. According to the Survey of Professional Forecasters, a group that is polled each quarter by the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, projected the U.S. CPI to hit 6% for the first quarter. In the most recent forecast three months ago, the panel projected a consumer price index gain of just 2.7%. However, that was just before the U.S. and Israel launched attacks against Iran. For the full year, the group forecast the CPI rate at 3.5% for the all-items and 2.9% for core, which excludes volatile food and energy prices. That’s up from estimates of 2.6% for both in the prior survey done three months ago. Two inflation reports earlier this week also showed rising price pressures in the retail and wholesale markets, adding to bets that the U.S. Federal Reserve’s regime-change efforts might not be all that easy. US 10-year yields topped 4.5%, and with the Iran conflict showing no signs of ending, investors are beginning to get jittery that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz will further deepen the energy disruptions. Generally, when bond yields spike, investors tend to move away from equities, especially technology shares. A rise in yields raises the cost of borrowing for corporates, diminishing the current value of future earnings in analyst models. “Risk sentiment is being dented by a global rise in bond yields, driven by a combination of inflation concerns, expectations for central-bank hikes, and worries around government debt as countries look to cushion the impact of higher energy prices,” said Angelo Kourkafas, Senior Global Strategist at Edward Jones, in an interview to Bloomberg. Tesla (TSLA): Shares of Tesla slipped 4% on Friday amid a broad selloff in tech stocks, while concerns for the EV giant’s business in China weighed further on the stock. Starbucks (SBUX): Starbucks Corp on Friday announced its third round of job cuts, affecting 300 employees in the U.S., as the company continues its strategic turnaround efforts. Poet Technologies (POET): POET Technologies shares declined after the company disclosed plans to raise capital through a securities offering and announced long-time finance chief Thomas Mika’s decision to leave the company later this year. Microsoft (MSFT): Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman on Friday revealed that Pershing Square has acquired a new stake in Microsoft, adding that the firm will disclose the position in a 13F filing. Nvidia (NVDA): U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday said that China has not yet approved purchases of Nvidia’s H200 AI chips. Crude oil prices jumped on Friday, rising past $105 per barrel after Trump told Fox News that he is losing patience with Iran. Brent crude futures for July gained more than 3% to close at $109.26 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for June advanced more than 4% to settle at $105.42 per barrel, CNBC reported. Cisco (CSCO) share price jumped 2% on Friday and recorded its best week since 2001 as investors continued to cheer the networking hardware maker’s stellar quarterly earnings performance, which blasted past expectations. Cisco stated that its record third-quarter (Q3) performance was driven by a strong, broad-based demand for its products. CEO Chuck Robbins stated that the company’s performance during the quarter demonstrated its relevance in connecting with and securing AI technology. HSBC upgraded the software name to ‘buy’ from ‘hold’. It also hiked its price target on shares to $137 from $77, implying nearly 19% upside from Thursday’s close. “Looking ahead, the biggest growth drivers for Cisco will likely be hyperscaler AI build-outs and enterprise artificial intelligence networking upgrades, in addition to campus modernization as requirements for traffic, security, and latency increase, according to HSBC. “Despite gross margin pressure, management has credible offsets through pricing, tighter contract terms, supply chain commitments, [operational expenditure] discipline, and lower memory utilization within designs,” analyst Stephen Bersey said in a note to clients, accessed by CNBC. CSCO’s revenue increased 12% in the quarter ended April 25 to $15.8 billion from $14.15 billion a year earlier, beating expectations of $15.6 billion. Net income rose to $1.06 per share, above the $1.04 expected, according to data from Fiscal.ai. The networking hardware firm expects revenue for the quarter ending July to be $16.7 billion to $16.9 billion, above market expectations of $15.8 billion, according to Fiscal.ai. Excluding some items, earnings will be roughly $1.16 to $1.18 a share. Analysts expect a profit of $1.07 a share. “Networking is a critical enabler of, and bottleneck to, AI model performance. This leads to high spending on AI network infrastructure that supports growth for Cisco and its peers. We expect this trend to continue powerfully over the next five years,” a recent Morningstar Report said. The fallout from escalating energy prices has moved beyond the gas pump and into the corporate boardrooms of the nation’s largest retailers, as the latest earnings cycle reveals erosion of profit margins across the consumer discretionary sector. The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight Consumer Discretionary ETF (RSPD) has retreated 13% from its January highs, reflecting a sharp shift in market sentiment amid rising geopolitical tensions and energy costs, which are reshaping the retail landscape. The downturn marks a significant reversal for a sector that began the year with optimism. Since the onset of the conflict in Iran in late February, the dynamics governing consumer spending have been fundamentally altered by supply chain disruptions and a volatile energy market. Most discretionary companies are signaling concern about sales and margins. Only two discretionary companies mentioned a positive impact from higher oil on first-quarter earnings calls, while the rest mentioned negative impacts or struck a neutral tone, according to data from Trivariate Research’s Adam Parker, accessed by Barron’s. “We continue to recommend an Underweight in consumer discretionary, as we suspect [earnings] estimate achievability will be below average for the sector,” Parker wrote A primary driver of the sector's decline has been the rapid escalation of energy prices. Since the start of the Iran war, global oil benchmarks have seen substantial gains as the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to a significant portion of global trade. Brent crude futures rose to $107.06 per barrel on Friday, marking a more than 12% increase over the last month alone. In the United States, West Texas Intermediate (WTI) has surged past $102 per barrel. The rising cost of fuel has acted as a double-edged sword for discretionary firms, simultaneously increasing logistics costs and squeezing average households' disposable income. For many of the sector’s top constituents, the impact of oil has been most visible in "last-mile" delivery and supply chain logistics. Rising diesel and jet fuel prices have forced companies to choose between raising prices for an already inflation-weary consumer or absorbing the costs internally. Royal Caribbean expects fuel costs to be about $1.3 billion higher than its earlier full-year forecast of around $1.17 billion, based on current pump prices and after hedging, while many U.S. airline companies have raised concerns about higher jet fuel prices denting margins. Analysts at S&P Global, in a note, stated that the recent oil shock could push headline U.S. inflation toward 4%, double its 2% inflation target, but expect the disruption to be temporary. The Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight Consumer Discretionary ETF, which provides broader exposure by weighting each of its constituents equally, has seen its top-performing holdings from the start of the year give back much of their gains. Since the war began, the performance of major constituents has been hit by a combination of high interest rates and falling consumer confidence: While Amazon’s (AMZN) AWS cloud division continued to perform well, its core retail business felt the weight of the fuel spike. "Our guidance anticipates higher transportation costs related to fuel inflation…," said Brian Olsavsky, Amazon's Chief Financial Officer, during the Q1 earnings call. Higher interest rates and rising inflation have also weighed on the share prices and operating margins of other components of the ETF, like Home Depot (HD) and Carvana (CVNA). Compounding the sector's woes is a persistent inflationary environment that shows few signs of abating. According to data released Friday, a poll of top economic forecasters by the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia now projects the U.S. inflation rate to hit 6% in the second quarter. The fund stated that Xerox makes an interesting investment as it provides opportunities supported by its ongoing operational advancements, new balance sheet initiatives, and its position within the industry. STARTEEPO further added that, from its perspective, the company has been undergoing a transition focused on stabilizing revenues, strengthening margins, and improving its financial profile over time. It also stated that even incremental progress across these segments may contribute to a more balanced market perception. The fund said it intends to act as a "constructive, long-term shareholder" and may engage in discussions with Xerox's management and board regarding the company’s business strategy, capital structure, and opportunities to enhance shareholder value. In April, Xerox reported its first-quarter earnings with revenue of $1.85 billion, beating analysts’ estimates of $1.74 billion, while the adjusted net loss of $0.43 per share was wider than the Wall Street expectations of a loss of $0.27 per share. title: Microsoft Stock In For Some Relief? Board Member Scoops Up $2M In MSFT After Sharp Slide - Stocktwits
content: Microsoft Corp. board member John Stanton purchased nearly $2 million in company stock, according to an exchange filing on Wednesday, a move that may offer some reassurance to investors after the mega-cap has come under pressure amid concerns about AI-related capital spending. MSFT stock edged 0.2% higher in the after-market session and was climbing in overnight trading. Stanton acquired 5,000 shares of Microsoft at $397.35 on Wednesday. Hedge Vision, an X account that analyses insider trades, said the trade was the largest insider buying at Microsoft in 11 years. Stocktwits could not independently verify the claim immediately. Stanton, also the founder of private equity firm Trilogy Partnerships, now owns 83,905 Microsoft shares directly and another 3,622 through a family trust. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for MSFT held in the ‘bearish’ zone, even as members noticed the trade. The insider buy comes during a board selloff in technology shares, which has particularly pressured MSFT stock. Microsoft shares are down by over 27% since their Oct. 28 peak and down 17.4% so far this year, the most among the Magnificent stocks. Only Nvidia is in the green for 2026, with a modest 0.8% gain. Tech stocks, particularly software companies, have come under pressure amid fresh concerns that AI tools will reduce demand for niche software and disrupt tech business models.
